stepHints.found: The breach is on record and the clock is running.
stepHints.assess: Find out what happened, which systems and data were affected, and how many people. Write what you learn in the note.
stepHints.tell_board: Send the full report to the Data Protection Board of India within the report window. Write in the note what you sent and when. This app records it; it does not send it.

stepHints.close: Close the breach once the Board and the affected people have been told and the work is done. A closed breach can no longer be changed.

setup.title: How to set this up in Azure
setup.intro: You need an app registration that can only read. This takes about five minutes in the Azure portal.

steps.register: In Microsoft Entra ID, open App registrations and choose New registration. Name it DPDP Kit and keep it single tenant.
steps.ids: On its Overview page, copy the Application (client) ID and the Directory (tenant) ID.
steps.secret: Under Certificates and secrets, make a new client secret and copy its value now. It is shown only once.
steps.reader: On your subscription, open Access control (IAM) and add the Reader role for the app. Copy the Subscription ID from the subscription’s Overview.
steps.graph: On the app, open API permissions, add Microsoft Graph application permissions AuditLog.Read.All, Policy.Read.All and Directory.Read.All, and choose Grant admin consent.

setup.note: Only these read permissions are used. Without the Graph permissions, the sign-in checks are skipped and the rest still run. The multi-factor report also needs a Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 licence.

questions.written_policy: You have a written privacy policy that senior management has approved.
questions.grievance_officer: You have named someone to handle complaints, and published how to reach them.
questions.consent_before_collecting: You ask for clear, specific consent before you collect personal data.
questions.notice_when_collecting: You tell people what you collect and why, in plain language, at the moment you collect it.
questions.withdraw_consent: People can withdraw their consent as easily as they gave it, and the steps are written down.
questions.access_to_data: People can ask for a copy of the personal data you hold about them.
questions.correct_data: People can ask you to correct their data when it is wrong or out of date.
questions.erase_data: People can ask you to delete their data, and you have a way to do it.
questions.data_inventory: You keep a list of the personal data your company collects and uses.
questions.purposes_written_down: For each kind of data on that list, the reason you collect it is written down.
questions.know_where_data_lives: You know where personal data is stored and who can reach it.
questions.access_controls: The systems that hold personal data are protected by logins and access controls.
questions.encryption: Personal data is encrypted when it is stored and when it is sent.
questions.security_reviews: You check the security of those systems on a regular schedule.
questions.processor_agreements: Every company that handles personal data for you has signed a data agreement.
questions.vendor_reviews: You review how those vendors protect data at least once a year.
questions.transfers_abroad: You know which vendors send personal data outside India, and you disclose it.
questions.breach_procedure: You have a written plan for what to do if personal data is breached.
questions.report_within_window: You could tell the Data Protection Board and the people affected within the legal time.
questions.retention_schedule: You have a retention schedule, and you delete data once its purpose is done.
questions.age_check: You check whether the people whose data you collect are under 18.
questions.parental_consent: Where you handle children's data, you get verifiable consent from a parent.
questions.harm_scenarios: You have listed the ways your use of data could seriously harm someone.
questions.sensitive_data_consent: You do not use sensitive data, such as financial, health or location data, without clear consent.

entra_mfa_registered.passRule: Every member of your organisation has registered at least one multi-factor method.
entra_mfa_registered.failRule: At least one member has not.
entra_mfa_registered.why: A stolen password alone should not be enough to sign in. The Act asks for reasonable security safeguards (section 8(5)).
entra_mfa_registered.fix: In Entra ID, open Protection, then Authentication methods, then Activity, then User registration details. Filter to users who have not registered, and ask them to register at aka.ms/mfasetup. A registration campaign can nudge them.

entra_mfa_enforced.passRule: Security defaults are on, or an enabled conditional access policy requires multi-factor authentication for all users.
entra_mfa_enforced.why: Registering a second step does nothing if signing in never asks for it.
entra_mfa_enforced.fix: Turn on security defaults under Entra ID, Properties, Manage security defaults. Or create a conditional access policy for All users that grants access only with multi-factor authentication.

entra_admin_count.passRule: Between two and five people hold the Global Administrator role.
entra_admin_count.failRule: One person holds it, or more than five.
entra_admin_count.why: One administrator is a single point of failure, and many is a lot of power in the accounts attackers aim for.
entra_admin_count.fix: Under Entra ID, Roles and administrators, Global Administrator: add a second account, or remove people who do not need it and give them a narrower role.

rbac_privileged.passRule: At most five accounts hold Owner or User Access Administrator over the whole subscription.
rbac_privileged.why: These roles can change anything, or hand that power to others.
rbac_privileged.fix: Under the subscription’s Access control (IAM), Role assignments: remove the ones that are not needed, move them to a resource group, or use time-limited access with Privileged Identity Management.

rbac_wildcard_roles.passRule: No custom role lists * (every action) in its permissions.
rbac_wildcard_roles.why: A role that allows everything is Owner under another name, and is easy to miss in a review.
rbac_wildcard_roles.fix: Under the subscription’s Access control (IAM), Roles: edit the custom role so that it lists only the actions it needs.

rbac_service_principals.passRule: No app holds Owner, User Access Administrator or Contributor over the whole subscription.
rbac_service_principals.why: Whoever holds an app’s secret has its power, and secrets are copied and leaked more easily than people’s sign-ins.
rbac_service_principals.fix: Under the subscription’s Access control (IAM), Role assignments: filter by Service principal and replace broad roles with narrower ones, scoped to the resource group the app needs.

storage_secure_transfer.passRule: Every storage account requires HTTPS and a minimum TLS version of 1.2 or newer.
storage_secure_transfer.failRule: An account allows plain HTTP, or an older TLS version.
storage_secure_transfer.why: Personal data sent without encryption can be read by anyone on the path. The Act asks for reasonable security safeguards (section 8(5)).
storage_secure_transfer.fix: Open the storage account, then Settings, Configuration. Set Secure transfer required to Enabled and Minimum TLS version to 1.2.

storage_public_access.passRule: No storage account allows anonymous public access to blobs.
storage_public_access.why: A public container can be read by anyone who has the address, with no sign-in.
storage_public_access.fix: Open the storage account, then Settings, Configuration. Set Allow Blob anonymous access to Disabled, and check that each container’s access level is Private.

storage_network_access.passRule: Every storage account accepts connections only from selected networks, or has public network access off.
storage_network_access.failRule: An account accepts connections from every network.
storage_network_access.why: A firewall narrows who can even try to reach the data, which limits the damage of a leaked key.
storage_network_access.fix: Open the storage account, then Security and networking, Networking. Choose Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, or Disabled, and add the networks that need access.

encryption_at_rest.passRule: Storage accounts, managed disks and SQL databases are encrypted at rest.
encryption_at_rest.why: Encryption at rest protects the data if a disk or a backup is taken. The Act asks for reasonable security safeguards (section 8(5)).
encryption_at_rest.fix: Azure encrypts by default, so something was turned off on purpose. Turn it back on: on a storage account under Encryption, and on a SQL database under Transparent data encryption.

keyvault_soft_delete.passRule: Soft delete is on for every key vault.
keyvault_soft_delete.failRule: It is off for a vault.
keyvault_soft_delete.why: Without it, a deleted vault or key is gone for good.
keyvault_soft_delete.fix: Soft delete cannot be switched off on new vaults. Recreate an old vault that lacks it, after copying its contents.

keyvault_purge_protection.passRule: Purge protection is on for every key vault.
keyvault_purge_protection.failRule: It is not for a vault.
keyvault_purge_protection.why: Without it, someone with access can destroy a deleted vault or key before its retention ends.
keyvault_purge_protection.fix: Open the key vault, then Properties, and set Purge protection to Enable. It cannot be turned off afterwards, so choose the retention period first.

keyvault_public_access.passRule: Every key vault has public network access disabled, or a firewall that denies by default.
keyvault_public_access.failRule: A vault is open to every network.
keyvault_public_access.why: Keys and secrets should be reachable only from the networks that use them.
keyvault_public_access.fix: Open the key vault, then Networking. Choose Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, or Disabled with a private endpoint, and add the networks that need access.

keyvault_rbac.passRule: Every key vault uses Azure role-based access control.
keyvault_rbac.failRule: A vault still uses access policies kept on the vault.
keyvault_rbac.why: Roles are reviewed in one place with the rest of your access, instead of on each vault separately.
keyvault_rbac.fix: Open the key vault, then Access configuration. Switch the permission model to Azure role-based access control, after copying each access policy to a role assignment.

data_in_india.passRule: Every data store is in an Indian region.
data_in_india.failRule: A data store is in another region.
data_in_india.why: The Act lets personal data go abroad unless the government restricts a country, but you should know where it is, for your records of processing and for your notice.
data_in_india.fix: Review each store listed. If its data should stay in India, move or recreate it in Central India, South India or West India. If abroad is intended, record it in your transfer register.

sql_tls.passRule: Every SQL server’s minimum TLS version is 1.2 or newer.
sql_tls.failRule: A server accepts an older version.
sql_tls.why: Older TLS versions have known weaknesses.
sql_tls.fix: Open the SQL server, then Security, Networking, Connectivity. Set Minimum TLS version to 1.2.

sql_public_access.passRule: Every SQL server has public network access disabled.
sql_public_access.why: A database on the public internet can be attacked by anyone, and its firewall rules and logins are the only defence.
sql_public_access.fix: Open the SQL server, then Security, Networking. Set Public network access to Disable and use private endpoints, or keep it on with tight firewall rules.

sql_firewall.passRule: No SQL server has a firewall rule that opens it to every address or to every Azure service.
sql_firewall.failRule: A server has a rule from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 (every address, a failure) or from 0.0.0.0 to 0.0.0.0 (every Azure service, a warning).
sql_firewall.why: A rule open to everyone makes the database reachable from anywhere, and every Azure service includes other people’s subscriptions.
sql_firewall.fix: Open the SQL server, then Security, Networking, Firewall rules. Delete the open rule and add rules for the addresses that need access.

sql_auditing.passRule: Auditing is on for every SQL server.
sql_auditing.failRule: It is off for a server.
sql_auditing.why: An audit log is how a breach is investigated afterwards, and the Act’s breach duties depend on knowing what happened.
sql_auditing.fix: Open the SQL server, then Security, Auditing. Switch on Azure SQL auditing and send it to a storage account or a Log Analytics workspace.

flexible_servers_tls.passRule: Every PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible server requires encrypted connections with TLS 1.2 or newer.
flexible_servers_tls.failRule: A server allows unencrypted connections or older TLS.
flexible_servers_tls.why: Database traffic should not travel in the clear. The Act asks for reasonable security safeguards (section 8(5)).
flexible_servers_tls.fix: Open the server, then Settings, Server parameters. Set require_secure_transport to ON, and set ssl_min_protocol_version (PostgreSQL) or tls_version (MySQL) to TLS 1.2 or newer.

datastores_public_access.passRule: No PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis or Cosmos DB service allows public network access.
datastores_public_access.why: As with SQL, a database on the public internet depends only on its firewall and logins.
datastores_public_access.fix: Open each service’s Networking page and use private access, or restrict public access to the addresses that need it.

cosmos_key_access.passRule: Every Cosmos DB account disables key-based access (local authentication).
cosmos_key_access.why: Keys can be copied and cannot be tied to a person, while sign-in with Entra ID can be taken back.
cosmos_key_access.fix: Open the Cosmos DB account, then Keys, and set Local authentication to Disabled, after moving apps to Entra ID sign-in.

cosmos_failover.passRule: Every Cosmos DB account with more than one region fails over automatically.
cosmos_failover.failRule: An account with several regions does not.
cosmos_failover.why: Without it, a regional failure means someone must act before the data is available again.
cosmos_failover.fix: Open the Cosmos DB account, then Replicate data globally, and turn on Automatic failover.

cosmos_backup.passRule: Every Cosmos DB account keeps continuous backups, or periodic backups for a week or more.
cosmos_backup.failRule: An account keeps periodic backups for less than a week.
cosmos_backup.why: A short backup window leaves little time to notice a problem and restore.
cosmos_backup.fix: Open the Cosmos DB account, then Backup and restore. Raise the retention, or switch to continuous backup.

webapp_https.passRule: Every web app and function app accepts only HTTPS.
webapp_https.failRule: An app also accepts plain HTTP.
webapp_https.why: Anything sent over plain HTTP, including sign-ins, can be read on the way.
webapp_https.fix: Open the app, then Settings, Configuration, General settings. Set HTTPS Only to On.

webapp_tls.passRule: Every web app’s minimum TLS version is 1.2 or newer.
webapp_tls.failRule: An app accepts an older version.
webapp_tls.why: Older TLS versions have known weaknesses.
webapp_tls.fix: Open the app, then Settings, Configuration, General settings. Set Minimum inbound TLS version to 1.2.

webapp_remote_debugging.passRule: Remote debugging is off for every web app.
webapp_remote_debugging.failRule: It is on for an app.
webapp_remote_debugging.why: A debugger that can be attached from outside is a way in to the code and its data.
webapp_remote_debugging.fix: Open the app, then Settings, Configuration, General settings. Set Remote debugging to Off.

webapp_ftp.passRule: No web app allows plain FTP.
webapp_ftp.why: Plain FTP sends the deployment password and the files in the clear.
webapp_ftp.fix: Open the app, then Settings, Configuration, General settings. Set FTP state to FTPS only, or Disabled.

webapp_identity.passRule: Every web app has a managed identity.
webapp_identity.why: An identity lets the app reach other services without a password kept in its settings, which could leak.
webapp_identity.fix: Open the app, then Settings, Identity. Switch on a system-assigned managed identity and give it only the roles it needs.

vm_identity.passRule: Every virtual machine has a managed identity.
vm_identity.why: An identity lets a machine reach other services without a password kept on it.
vm_identity.fix: Open the virtual machine, then Security, Identity. Switch on a system-assigned managed identity and give it only the roles it needs.

vm_ssh_password.passRule: No Linux virtual machine accepts password sign-in.
vm_ssh_password.why: A password on a machine reachable from the internet is guessed at all day.
vm_ssh_password.fix: Use SSH keys. Set PasswordAuthentication no in the machine’s sshd configuration, or recreate it with key-only sign-in.

vm_secure_boot.passRule: No virtual machine has secure boot turned off.
vm_secure_boot.why: Secure boot stops tampered start-up software from running.
vm_secure_boot.fix: Open the virtual machine’s Configuration and enable Trusted launch with Secure boot, on a size that supports it.

aks_rbac.passRule: Every Kubernetes cluster uses role-based access control.
aks_rbac.why: Without it, any credential can do anything in the cluster.
aks_rbac.fix: Role-based access cannot be turned off on new clusters. Recreate an old cluster with it enabled.

aks_aad.passRule: Every cluster signs people in with Microsoft Entra ID.
aks_aad.why: Sign-in with work accounts can be switched off when someone leaves, unlike a shared credential.
aks_aad.fix: Open the cluster, then Settings, Cluster configuration. Enable Microsoft Entra authentication with Azure RBAC.

aks_network_policy.passRule: Every cluster has a network policy.
aks_network_policy.why: Without one, any workload can talk to any other, so one break-in spreads.
aks_network_policy.fix: Create the cluster with a network policy (Azure or Calico), or add one to an existing cluster.

aks_private_api.passRule: Every cluster’s control point is private, or limited to listed addresses.
aks_private_api.failRule: A cluster’s control point is open to every address.
aks_private_api.why: The control point is the most powerful door into a cluster.
aks_private_api.fix: Open the cluster, then Networking. Enable a private cluster, or set Authorized IP ranges.

aks_policy_addon.passRule: Every cluster has the Azure Policy add-on.
aks_policy_addon.why: It checks what runs in a cluster against your rules.
aks_policy_addon.fix: Open the cluster, then Settings, Policies, and enable the Azure Policy add-on.

aks_auto_upgrade.passRule: Every cluster has an automatic upgrade channel.
aks_auto_upgrade.why: A cluster that is not upgraded falls behind on security fixes.
aks_auto_upgrade.fix: Open the cluster, then Settings, Cluster configuration. Set an Automatic upgrade channel such as Stable or Patch.

aks_monitoring.why: Monitoring records what a cluster is doing, which an investigation needs.
aks_monitoring.fix: Open the cluster, then Monitoring. Enable Container insights or Azure Monitor managed metrics.

acr_admin_user.passRule: No container registry has the admin user on.
acr_admin_user.why: A shared login cannot be tied to a person, and its password is usually copied around.
acr_admin_user.fix: Open the registry, then Settings, Access keys. Turn Admin user off, and sign in with Entra ID or a service principal with a role such as AcrPull.

acr_public_access.passRule: No container registry allows public network access.
acr_public_access.why: Images can hold secrets and show how your systems are built.
acr_public_access.fix: Open the registry, then Settings, Networking. Disable public access and use a private endpoint, or restrict it to selected addresses (Premium).

acr_anonymous_pull.passRule: No container registry allows anonymous pulls.
acr_anonymous_pull.why: Anyone could pull your images without signing in.
acr_anonymous_pull.fix: Open the registry, then Settings, Properties, and turn off Anonymous pull access.

acr_content_trust.passRule: Every Premium container registry uses content trust.
acr_content_trust.why: Signed images stop a tampered image from being used.
acr_content_trust.fix: Open the registry, then Policies, Content trust, and enable it. It is a Premium feature.

acr_retention.passRule: Every Premium container registry has a retention policy.
acr_retention.why: Old untagged images pile up and may hold weaknesses and data nobody needs.
acr_retention.fix: Open the registry, then Policies, Retention. Enable it and choose how many days to keep untagged images.

nsg_open_ports.passRule: No network security group allows inbound traffic from anywhere to SSH, remote desktop, database ports or all ports.
nsg_open_ports.why: Login and database ports facing the internet are attacked constantly.
nsg_open_ports.fix: Open the network security group, then Inbound security rules. Change the source from Any (or Internet) to your own addresses or a service tag, or delete the rule.

environment_separation.passRule: Resource groups for production and for non-production both exist, told apart by an environment tag or by name.
environment_separation.why: Keeping production apart limits what a mistake or a test can reach.
environment_separation.fix: Tag each resource group with environment set to production, staging or dev, or name it that way. For stronger separation use separate subscriptions.

monitor_alerts.passRule: Alerts exist for changes to policy assignments, security solutions, network security groups and SQL firewall rules.
monitor_alerts.failRule: One or more of them has no alert.
monitor_alerts.why: Someone should be told when the rules that protect the environment change.
monitor_alerts.fix: Under Azure Monitor, Alerts, create an Activity log alert for each missing change listed, with an action group that notifies the right people.

monitor_log_export.passRule: The subscription’s activity log is exported to a workspace, a storage account or an event hub.
monitor_log_export.why: Azure keeps the activity log for only 90 days, and the Act’s breach duties may need older records.
monitor_log_export.fix: Under Monitor, Activity log, Export activity logs, add a diagnostic setting that sends it to a Log Analytics workspace or a storage account.

policy_assignments.passRule: At least one Azure Policy is assigned to the subscription.
policy_assignments.why: Policies enforce your rules on every new resource, instead of relying on people remembering.
policy_assignments.fix: Under Policy, Assignments, assign a built-in initiative such as the Microsoft cloud security benchmark.

defender_plans.passRule: Every Defender for Cloud plan is on.
defender_plans.why: Each plan watches one kind of resource for threats and weaknesses. They cost money, so turning on all of them is a choice to make.
defender_plans.fix: Under Defender for Cloud, Environment settings, your subscription: switch on the plans for the kinds of resource you use.

defender_recommendations.passRule: Defender for Cloud has no unhealthy recommendations.
defender_recommendations.failRule: It has some. High severity counts as a failure.
defender_recommendations.why: These are Microsoft’s own findings about your resources.
defender_recommendations.fix: Under Defender for Cloud, Recommendations, work through them by severity. Each has steps or a Remediate button.

remove.body: The key is forgotten. Files cannot be read until it is set up again.

ai.privacy: When you add a policy from a file, its text is sent to the service you choose, with your key, to be read. DPDP Kit does not keep the file. A person always checks and approves what it suggests.
